title: Born in Stockton, raised in Tracy; grandfathers and ancestry
summary: Maxwell describes the semi-desert San Joaquin Valley, a large household with grandfathers and uncles, and Scotch-Irish, Creole and Civil War ancestors.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, I was born in Stockton, California although my family lived in Tracy. This is in the San Joaquin Valley in California. It was 1917*and the area then was semi-desert. There was no irrigation or anything at that time and it was very desolate. But it was beautiful countryside. I appreciated it more after I left. And as a child, we were three or four miles from the nearest neighbor so I played mostly with animals. Had a pet snake, pet chicken, pet dog, cat and things of that kind.
However, we had a big family. We lived with my grandfather and my great grandfather, two or three uncles and cousins, so there was always a lot of people around. And my great
grandfather had fought in the Civil War and was found of telling about the time he'd seen Lincoln.

Well, his name was Reid (PHONETIC), too. See, my grandfather's name was Gilmore Reid and I'm trying to think of my great grandfather's first name. I really can't think of it at the moment. And they came from -- my mother's side, this was my grandfather Reid, great grandfather Reid was Scotch Irish and his wife was, I believe, German Jewish. And on my mother's mother's side her father was Scotch Irish, he was from New Orleans and he was an artist there and when the Civil War started he went up to New York to join the Northern army.

My mother's name was Margaret Mary Reid. And this great grandfather said he was married to what was called a Creole woman, which means she was French, Spanish, Indian -- I don't know what. But judging from the pictures she was dark, some kind, which was probably the reason he went to the North when the Civil War started.

I have pictures of them. So we -- there was no electricity in those days so no radio or anything. In the evenings people sat around and sang songs. Everybody played musical instruments. So from as far back as I can remember,
